sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/get-started/overview-of-formulas-in-excel

In Excel's A1 notation, letters identify columns and numbers identify rows. When a formula is copied or filled, a relative reference preserves its offset from the formula cell: its row and column adjust with the copy displacement. A dollar sign fixes the component immediately following it. An absolute reference fixes both components; a mixed reference fixes only its column or only its row. Each reference in a formula follows its own anchors. These are copying/filling rules for ordinary cell references; cutting or moving cells, structural edits and structured table references are outside this summary.

items.prompt: A sales summary has regions in B2:E2 (North, South, East, West) and quarters in A3:A6 (Q1-Q4). Cell B3 should multiply the quarter factor in $A$1 by the regional target in $B$1, then fill across to E3 and down to E6. What should B3 contain?
items.topic: Combine relative, absolute and mixed A1 referenc

choice_reasons.reason: The quarter factor should come from $A$1 (fixed cell), but $A1 has a relative row — filling down changes it to $A2, $A3, etc., reading wrong cells. Also the regional target should be from $B$1 but B$1 fixes only the row; filling across changes the column (C$1, D$1), which would read regional targets correctly but the quarter factor anchor is wrong.

$A$1 is the fixed quarter factor (correct). B1 has a relative row — filling down changes it to B2, B3, etc., reading wrong cells instead of the fixed regional target row. $A$3 fixes the quarter column and row, so filling down won't adjust the quarter factor from A3:A6. This is incorrect.

$A$1 is the fixed quarter factor cell (correct, stays fixed). B$1 fixes row 1 so the regional target row stays fixed; filling across changes B to C, D, E (correct regional targets). $A3 fixes column A so the quarter factor column stays A; filling down changes row 3 to 4,5,6 (correct quarters). All three relationships are preserved.

$A$1 is fixed (correct). $B$1 fixes both column and row of the regional target — filling across to C3, D3, E3 always uses B1 instead of C1, D1, E1. The regional target column must be relative. A3 has a relative column — filling across changes it to B3, C3, reading wrong cells for the quarter factor.

sourceDocuments.text:

A scale written 1:n relates one unit on the map to n of the same units on the ground. Convert units consistently before comparing distances. A straight measurement between endpoints represents their direct separation; measuring a winding route requires following its bends. Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/get-started/overview-of-formulas-in-excel

In Excel's A1 notation, letters identify columns and numbers identify rows. When a formula is copied or filled, a relative reference preserves its offset from the formula cell: its row and column adjust with the copy displacement. A dollar sign fixes the component immediately following it. An absolute reference fixes both components; a mixed reference fixes only its column or only its row. Each reference in a formula follows its own anchors. These are copying/filling rules for ordinary cell references; cutting or moving cells, structural edits and structured table references are outside this summary.

items.prompt: A commission sheet has rates in A1:A5 and sales amounts in B1:F1. Cell B2 needs =A2*B1 so it can fill across to F2 and down to B5, always using the correct rate and amount. What should B2 contain?
items.topic: Combine relative, absolute and mixed A1 referenc

choice_reasons.reason: Filling across: A2 column shifts right, so rates column A is lost. Filling down: B1 row shifts down, so amounts row 1 is lost. Both references are fully relative and break when copied.

$A locks column A (rates) so filling across keeps the correct rate; row 2 is relative so filling down picks the correct rate row. B is relative so filling across picks the correct amount column; $1 locks row 1 so filling down keeps the amounts row. This is the correct mixed-reference formula.
$2 locks row 2 for rates (wrong when filling down) and $B locks column B for amounts (wrong when filling across). This is the opposite of what is needed.
$A$2 locks both row and column of the rate, so filling down always uses A2's rate instead of the correct row's rate.
